wu: Job Charades: Students act out jobs (doctor, teacher, engineer) while others guess. Props: job flashcards. They shout 'You're a ___!' when correct.
wuAlt: Job Pictionary: Draw jobs on the board; classmates guess the job name.
Word Association: Start with 'job'—students say one related word each (e.g., 'hospital,' 'uniform,' 'salary').
pres: Show job ads with 'have to' (e.g., 'Teachers have to work hard'). Model 'The more experience you have, the more jobs you can get.' Check understanding with thumbs up/down for true/false sentences.
presAlt: Use a story about two jobs (e.g., 'Ali is a chef; he has to stand all day. Sara is a writer; she doesn't have to travel.')
Realia: Bring in items related to jobs (stethoscope, laptop) and elicit 'have to' sentences.
prac: Job Comparison Grid: Students fill in a table comparing two jobs (e.g., hours, salary) using 'have to' and 'the more..., the more...' in pairs. Support with sentence starters.
pracAlt: Find Someone Who...: Survey classmates about jobs using 'Do you have to...?' questions.
Double Comparative Race: Write sentences like 'The more you study, the more opportunities you get' on the board; students race to copy them correctly.
ls: Listen to a podcast clip about dream jobs. Students note down 3 jobs mentioned and 1 'have to' requirement for each. Check answers in pairs.
re: Job Relay: Teams race to write 'the more..., the more...' sentences on the board about jobs (e.g., 'The more creative you are, the better artist you are').
prod: Dream Job Debate: Students work in pairs to prepare a 2-minute talk comparing their current job/studies to their dream job using 'have to' and double comparatives. Present to the class.
rw: Read a short job profile of a Moroccan engineer. Underline 3 job collocations (e.g., 'work long hours,' 'solve problems'). Then write 3 sentences about your ideal job using these collocations.
st: Read a short story about a teen choosing between two jobs. End with the goodbye routine: 'Today we compared jobs using double comparatives—great job! Thank you, class.'
g: Students mark off jobs on a bingo card as the teacher describes them using 'have to'.
Students sit in a circle; each adds a clause to a growing sentence (e.g., 'The more I learn... the more I earn...').
Teams take turns acting out jobs; fastest to guess gets a point.
Match job words with collocations (e.g., 'doctor' + 'work night shifts').
Ask 3 classmates about their dream job and write down their answers.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 40-word paragraph comparing two jobs using 3+ double comparatives.
Support learners: Use a sentence frame: 'The more ___ you have, the more ___ you get.'
hw: Write a KET-style email (25+ words) to a friend about your dream job, using 'have to' and one double comparative.
Create a poster for your dream job with 3 'have to' requirements and 1 double comparative sentence.
Record a 30-second voice note describing why you want your dream job, using 'the more..., the more...'.
tip: Pair stronger with weaker learners during the production task to build confidence—teens often learn best from peers.
